story.headline: Oil fell about 3% overnight, with Brent near $110 a barrel, as Iranian negotiators held a third day of talks in Qatar. Currencies barely moved before rate decisions in Australia and Britain and US elections.

reads.policy: Most central banks still lean toward higher rates because energy keeps inflation high, and this week Australia and Britain are both expected to raise them. With those hikes mostly priced, their currencies will move on whether the banks hint at more. In the US, bets on a December Fed hike held firm.
reads.growth: China sent mixed signals: the official factory survey slipped into decline, but a private survey of smaller firms stayed solid. That leaves Australia and New Zealand without a clear push either way. US factory figures later today give the first look at how the US economy began the autumn quarter.
reads.inflation: Cheaper oil overnight eased some of the fear that energy will keep pushing prices up. But inflation is still well above target in the US, the euro area, Britain and Australia, so central banks have little room to relax. Euro-area figures on Wednesday are the week's main inflation test.
reads.risk: Markets started November calmer after October's tech share slide, and the weekend passed without a US strike on Iran. That cut demand for the safe-haven yen and franc. Attacks on Gulf shipping continue, so the calm could break quickly.
reads.tot: Oil fell as talks in Qatar raised hopes of ending the US–Iran war. That trims the boost oil exporters like Canada get, and eases the cost for importers like Japan and the euro area. Prices are still high by historical standards, so the gap between winners and losers remains.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and cheaper oil now takes some pressure off those bets. They are also betting against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Their large bets on gold are shrinking, and their bets on oil rising are among the weakest in a decade.
reads.fiscal: Fitch joined Moody's in putting France's credit rating on negative outlook, which keeps a weight on the euro. France's parliament votes on the revenue side of its budget on Tuesday. Canada presents its budget on Thursday.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and two more officials have since called for further hikes. Markets see a December hike as likely, and those bets firmed slightly overnight.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and the economy is still growing fast.
fed.watch: This week's US factory and services surveys and Friday's October jobs report: strong figures would firm up a December hike.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. But the economy did not grow in July or August, which makes a second hike soon harder to justify.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, a bit less than even odds.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation and the bank raised its forecasts sharply, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem's speeches on Tuesday and Thursday, Canada's budget on Thursday and October jobs figures on Friday, plus oil prices.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, but it says more tightening is likely, and markets lean toward a December hike. Saturday's election adds uncertainty for the kiwi.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, and firms say they plan to raise prices more.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand job figures at 3:45 PM CT Tuesday, the general election on Saturday, November 7, and the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. Worries over France's debt, now on negative outlook at two rating firms, weigh on the euro.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, and the economy grew faster than expected over the summer.
ecb.watch: Euro-area inflation for October at 4:00 AM CT Wednesday, and France's budget vote on Tuesday.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, with one member voting to hike, and said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. Governor Kazuo Ueda named no date, but a December hike looks likely and would give the yen some support.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy and the jobs market tight.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech at 10:00 AM CT Friday, Japanese wage and price figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates to 4.85% tonight, the highest since 2008, after inflation ran hotter than it forecast. With the hike mostly priced, the Aussie will move on whether it signals more.
rba.why: Underlying inflation is running above the bank's own forecasts, and business-level prices are still climbing.
rba.watch: The decision at 9:30 PM CT on Monday, November 2, and Governor Michele Bullock's press conference an hour later.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and the debate is already about December. Firms now expect faster price rises, which makes the hike easier to justify.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, with service prices still sticky.
boe.watch: The decision at 6:00 AM CT on Thursday, November 5, and whether the bank hints at a second hike in December.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation is low, so the franc mostly moves on global fear and calm.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is below target, so the bank has no reason to raise rates while others do.
snb.watch: Swiss inflation figures at 1:30 AM CT Tuesday and a speech by Chairman Martin Schlegel on Thursday; the next decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Cheaper oil, if it lasts, could ease some of that pressure.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, which keeps US rates high.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is uneven, energy imports cost more, and France's debt worries weigh on it. The European Central Bank still leans toward a hike in December, which gives it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth beat forecasts over the summer only thanks to Ireland; France shrank, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Prices are rising fast in Italy and France, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike, even as Germany cooled.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: Two of the three big rating firms now have France on negative outlook, which keeps investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound scores well because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, inflation is high and the economy is holding up. It is near its strongest against the euro this year.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the pound, so a firm Bank of England could force them to buy it back.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. The Bank of Japan says inflation has reached its goal, so a December hike could start to change that.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is still far below others', though it says inflation has reached its goal, which points to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, and Tokyo's warnings limit how weak it gets.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators holding unusually big bets on the yen, which could unwind fast if it weakens.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is below target, which keeps the Swiss National Bank from raising rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, though high oil has dulled that pull lately.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates tonight and high commodity prices bring money in. A weakening job market is the main drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3, which supports the Aussie.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected, which keeps hikes coming.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money into the country.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the Aussie, so a firm rate hike could force them to buy it back.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and high oil prices bring money in. Growth is the soft spot: the economy has stalled, and oil's overnight fall trims its support.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and may do so again in December, which narrows the gap with US rates.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money in, though oil fell on hopes of an end to the Iran war.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is weak after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, and Saturday's election adds uncertainty. A steady services sector and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, and business confidence rose in October.
notes.risk: The kiwi has held up reasonably well through recent share market swings.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so good news could force them to buy it back.
